newsitem.title: USA: Fujitsu to ship flat-panel monitor to U.S..
newsitem.headline: Fujitsu to ship flat-panel monitor to U.S..

text.p: Fujitsu General America, a leader in plasma display technology, said Tuesday it will ship to the U.S. the world's largest hang-on-the-wall computer and television monitor, Plasmavision 42.
Marketing and sales will be done through its new reprsentative, Pixelworks of Portland, Ore.
With a 42-inch diagonal screen size, Plasmavision 42 is the first large-format, flat-panel plasma display to be shipped to the U.S., the company said.
The company said the new product features built-in capabilities allowing it to function as a large-format monitor for both video and computer graphics.

With a depth of less than six inches, the display is slim enough to hang on a wall, making it useful in business presentations, entertainment centers, and public display applications such as kiosks and promotional signage, it said.
"We believe the Plasmavision 42 will have an important impact in both the business and home markets," said Brad Zenger, vice president of marketing and sales for Pixelworks.
Suggested U.S. list price is $13,999, it said.

Among its advantages, it said, is that Plasmavision technology generates its own light, versus reflecting it from a screen. Because of this, it said, the device is easily viewable in any ambient light condition.
Furthermore, it said that with a viewing angle of 160 degrees both horizontally and vertically, the product can be placed in the room and everyone can enjoy a perfect image.
It said Plasmavision 42 is the first product designed for "digital convergence," the convergence of the computer world and television.
It is the only device capable of seamlessly displaying any type of graphical information and entertainment media regardless of sources such as a personal computer or video.

In addition, an advanced feature of the display allows it to take an incoming standard video or computer graphics input and resize it for the wide-screen format on-the-fly, with no visual "artifacts," it said.
